turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you too, Dr. Smith. Um, I'm here because I just can't stop focusing on my face. Specifically, the left side of my face looks really uneven and puffy to me. 

I notice it constantly, especially on video calls for work, and in photos from my salsa classes. The thing is, everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything wrong or that they don't know what I'm talking about, but I just can't stop looking at it. It's... well, it's really starting to mess with my work and my social life, so I figured I needed to talk to someone about it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes a constant preoccupation with perceived unevenness and puffiness on the left side of their face, which others say they cannot see.

turns.doctor_question: When people tell you they don't see what you see, do you ever consider the possibility that your perception of your face might be inaccurate, or are you completely certain that the puffiness and unevenness are objectively there?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... I guess it's a little bit of both. When I look at myself, I am completely certain it's there. It just looks so obvious to me. 

But... since literally everyone tells me they don't see it, I do sometimes stop and wonder if maybe my mind is playing tricks on me, or if I'm blowing it out of proportion. It's just really hard to actually believe them when the puffiness feels so real every single time I look.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes a persistent focus on perceived facial puffiness and unevenness that others tell them they cannot see.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient demonstrates insight by admitting they sometimes wonder if their mind is playing tricks on them, indicating their belief is not entirely fixed or delusional.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself spending a significant amount of time checking your face in the mirror or asking others for reassurance about how you look?
turns.patient_response:
Yes, I do. A lot, actually. Before my work meetings or if I'm getting ready to go somewhere, I... well, I keep opening the camera preview on my phone or laptop. I'll sit there changing the angle and the lighting, just checking it. And I'm constantly fixing my hair around that left side of my face, trying to see if I can make it look better. 

I also end up retaking pictures of myself over and over. And I definitely ask my friends if I look strange. I do all of this so much that, honestly, half the time I end up making myself late, or I just get so drained from the whole process that I don't even want to go out anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors such as checking camera previews, fixing hair, retaking pictures, and seeking reassurance from friends about their appearance.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from checking in the mirror or asking for reassurance, do you ever feel compelled to touch, pick at, or try to 'fix' the skin or features on that side of your face?
turns.patient_response: Um, no, not really. I don't find myself picking at my skin or touching it a lot. It's... it's really just the looking, and like I mentioned, moving my hair around to try and hide the shape of it. But I don't actually try to physically mess with the skin or the features themselves. I just stare at it.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient confirms engaging in appearance-related repetitive behaviors, specifically staring at their features (checking) and moving their hair to hide the shape (camouflaging), even though they deny skin picking.
